name: Reilly's Law of Retail Gravitation
statement: A retail center attracts trade from a surrounding area in direct proportion to its size and in inverse proportion to the square of the distance to it.
statementAccent: in direct proportion to its size and in inverse proportion to the square of the distance
meaning: Reilly's law borrows the form of Newton's law of gravitation to describe shopping behavior: bigger cities or retail centers pull in customers from farther away than smaller ones, because size (analogous to mass) increases attractiveness while distance discourages travel with rapidly diminishing effect. It is used to locate the "breaking point" between two competing retail centers: the boundary where consumers are indifferent between traveling to one or the other.
mechanism: For two centers of population or retail size P_A and P_B separated by distance D, the point of indifference lies at distance d = D / (1 + √(P_B/P_A)) from center A. Where the two centers are equal in size, the breaking point falls exactly halfway; as one center grows larger, the breaking point shifts toward the smaller center, expanding the larger center's trade area.

examples.text: William J. Reilly formulated the law from his earlier 1929 research and published it formally in The Law of Retail Gravitation (1931), based on observed shopping-trip patterns between Texas cities.
Paul Converse later reformulated Reilly's law explicitly as a "breaking point" formula to delineate the trade-area boundary between two competing towns.
David Huff's probabilistic Huff model generalized Reilly's two-center law to multiple retail centers and multiple attributes, and is used in real retail site-selection analysis.

whyItMatters: It was an early and influential attempt to quantify retail trade-area boundaries, underpinning later, more sophisticated market-area and retail-location models still used in commercial site selection and regional retail planning.
limits: It assumes a flat, featureless geography with no rivers, highways, or other barriers, and assumes consumers are indifferent between cities except for size: ignoring modern factors like highway access, store variety, and behavioral effects on shopping trips.
misreadings: It is sometimes treated as a precise predictive law of consumer behavior rather than a simplified heuristic analogy borrowed from physics.
origin: Formulated by William J. Reilly in The Law of Retail Gravitation (1931), building on retail-trade research he had published in 1929 at the University of Texas. Reilly borrowed the form of Newton's gravitation directly, pull rising with size and falling with the square of distance, to predict which of two cities a town between them would shop in. It is the ancestor of the gravity models still used in trade and transport.

sources.text: Wikipedia's entry noting Reilly's law of retail gravitation is a heuristic developed by William J. Reilly in 1931 — supports the origin, year, and heuristic status.
The same article's statement of the breaking-point formula d = D / (1 + √(P_B/P_A)) — supports the gravitational mechanism and formula.
